Sure Julia, we're really just trying to estimate the underlying joint distribution of all the data. 

So, if you have columns X, Y, Z, A, B, C (often you have hundreds) then we're trying to learn the underlying distribution P(X, Y, Z, A, B, C). 

Of course, we're bayesians, so we're actually producing samples from the probability distribution on those distributions, that is, 

P(P(X, Y, Z, A, B, C) | observed data). 

We're using nested dirichlet processes -- the DP is a lovely nonparametric statistical object developed over the past several decades, which showed up in the machine learning community (yes, we're always behind) in about 2001, and has been used as a "prior on distributions" for quite some time. They actually compose well, so you can start talking about stochastic processes over richer spaces, like trees, table partitions, etc. 

And we solve it all with more-MCMC-than-you-can-shake-a-stick-at. Lots of samplers, lots of parallelism, lots of python and c++. 

 The nice thing is that, learning a distribution on the joint model, we can make flexible predictions that do a pretty decent job of respecting uncertainty, and handle missing data and heterogenous data types with ease. Then normal people can query it like a database. 


...Eric

Thanks. About the only info on their site:

https://www.priorknowledge.com/infer-structure

other than the puns ("infer-structure" and logo "p(k)")
is that they're using not only Bayesian non-parmetric MCMC
that's "massively scaled", but "some of the most advanced
ones in the world".

Google "Prediction" is in the same black-box,
cloud-based stats business:

https://developers.google.com/prediction/

What p(k) sent Julia was more informative, indicating they're
doing full joint models (as opposed to treating some columns
in a database as predictors):

>> ... we're really just trying to estimate the underlying joint distribution of all the data.

>>
>> So, if you have columns X, Y, Z, A, B, C (often you have hundreds) then we're trying to learn the underlying
>> distribution P(X, Y, Z, A, B, C).
>>
>> Of course, we're bayesians, so we're actually producing samples from the probability distribution on those
>> distributions, that is,
>>
>> P(P(X, Y, Z, A, B, C) | observed data).
>>
>> We're using nested dirichlet processes -- the DP is a lovely nonparametric statistical object developed over the past
>> several decades, which showed up in the machine learning community (yes, we're always behind) in about 2001, and has
>> been used as a "prior on distributions" for quite some time. They actually compose well, so you can start talking
>> about stochastic processes over richer spaces, like trees, table partitions, etc.
>>
>> And we solve it all with more-MCMC-than-you-can-shake-a-stick-at. Lots of samplers, lots of parallelism, lots of
>> python and c++.
>>
>> The nice thing is that, learning a distribution on the joint model, we can make flexible predictions that do a pretty
>> decent job of respecting uncertainty, and handle missing data and heterogenous data types with ease. Then normal
>> people can query it like a database.

I think they're selling applications and services, not
something to do general Bayesian modeling with.

There's some very high-level Python API info about
integrating with data(bases), and some stuff to download
and try without understanding how it works, but I don't
really have time to kick the tires.

- Bob

parts: Yes, I agree. I don't think they're creating a Stan-like product for others to use, I think they have a Stan-like engine that they're using to fit Dirichlet processes. We could of course let them know about Stan and then they can use it if they'd like. No big deal for now, I just thought I'd let you know.
